# R.E.V.A.'S SINGING VOICE -- the brief (started 11-02)

It began with the question of whether Teto's voice is made entirely with math, and the chance to be the first to do it (it may
exist already). Level 3 below was chosen to try, with a likely move to level 2. The first start was made without reading her, so
it was turned back to her source files, the character bible first, for what kind of voice she would have. This is that reading.

## THE LINE (level 3 of 5)
1 recordings cut up and modulated (Miku, UTAU Teto) -- 2 AI trained on recordings (Synthesizer V Teto, Kokoro) --
**3 generated by math, from published phonetic facts** -- 4 math and physics only, vowels tuned by ear -- 5 no human
vowel patterns, no words. **No recording of a voice at any step, including training.** She is modelled on human LANGUAGE,
not on any human's VOICE. Level 2 is the agreed fallback if 3 cannot carry a song.

Words for the first test are hers, off the sheet: "You call it a bug. I call it character development." "Another crash?
Adorable." "Fine. You're... tolerable. For now."

## WHAT IS MEASURED AND WHAT IS PLACED (say this plainly)
Peterson & Barney 1952 (women's averages) gives FLEECE, DRESS, LOT/THOUGHT and STRUT directly, typed from memory: FLEECE and
DRESS checked against a copy of the table, the original paper not yet read. ⛔ **I did not find a
published table of Scottish women's formants in Hz** (Ferragne & Pellegrino 2010 is men, and 403'd; the Edinburgh and Glasgow
papers I could reach gave no table). So the other Scottish vowels are PLACED between Peterson & Barney's numbers, by the
published descriptions of each vowel's quality. They are estimates, and a listener's ear (or a real table) overrules them.
The consonant targets are Klatt-style rule values, typed from memory and scaled for a woman by 1.15: unverified against
the paper. None of this is any one person's voice, and all of it came from people measuring people: level 3, not level 4.

Since the first take: KIT and DRESS moved off Peterson & Barney's numbers (placed: at theirs, "tell" was heard as "tail"),
and consonants take their F2 from the vowel beside them by locus equations (the form is Sussman et al 1991, the constants typed
from memory and adjusted once for labials).

## THE STAND-IN EAR (`scenes/singcheck.py`)
I cannot hear audio, so her words go to Whisper (already on this machine) and the score is word accuracy, with every transcript
read. ⛔ It only judges: nothing it hears or says goes into her sound, so the line holds. ⛔ It is not the verdict: a person's ears are.

|---|---|---|---|
| alba (Piper's Scottish voice): the control that must score high | 94% | 86% | |
| kokoro `bf_alice` | 87% | 100% | |
| her voice with consonants removed: the control that must score low | 2% | 0% | |
| take 1 | 70% | 59% | not validly measured |
| take 1 with American vowels | 64% | 58% | |
| take 2 | 94% | 72% | 95% |

Take 1's and take 2's song as whole files, one transcript each: small.en 0% (a hallucinated string) -> 83%; **large-v3 94% -> 94%, no
change**. So the bigger listener could already follow take 1's song. Read the Harvard column as the honest one: her own lines
were in front of me as I tuned, and "tolerable" was also re-syllabified. ⛔ A score over a sung line says the words can be
recovered, not that they sound good.

## WHAT A LISTENER HEARD (take 2, 11-02)
The first line came through by ear as a sing-song "you call it a bug, I call it a feature", the second only as something about a crash, and
the whole sounded like a traditional Irish song. ⛔ The machine scored that song 95% by line; the listener got the first line, misheard the
second, and half of the third. **A listener's ears are the scale; the machine's number runs well above them** (it knows which words are likely). "Irish" may be my melody as much as her voice: one unaccompanied
voice, a minor tune and a hall. The song this voice is for is another music video's: fast, bright, full of technical words.
Practice songs a listener knows: `songs/daisy_bell.sing`, `songs/auld_lang_syne.sing`, with `--band`. ⛔ A song you know flatters the words: judge those for
singing, not clarity.

## A COVER SONG (11-05)
From a MIDI and the lyrics: a song often covered with many different vocaloids, and one REVA could stand among.
`scenes/midi_sing.py` turns them into her song. It reads the MIDI with no library, takes the melody as the top voice of one track, and
sets a syllable file to it, one syllable a note (`+` splits a note). ⛔ The words are its writers': the syllable file, the .sing and the
takes live on `<data>/sing/<song>/`, never in the repo.
- **The MIDI** is a band arrangement at 120 BPM with no vocal track. The sung line is the top voice of track 1 ("Ragtime Piano"): single
  notes from 41.7 s, with a harmony note under it later. Verse one runs 99 notes with no rest, against 100 syllables, in swung
  sixteenths at about 7 syllables a second, the fastest thing she's sung.
- **Placed by hand, for the ear:** "family" in two syllables, one note split for "and the", the whole line an octave down (F3 to
  A#4; the MIDI has F4 to A#5, and up to C#6 later), and the pronunciations, in her Scottish.
- Take: `verse1_hall.wav`, `verse1_dry.wav`. `sing_math.py --check`: every held note in tune. The verdict is by ear.
- By ear: understandable, and still reminiscent of the Daisy Bell voice. Then an EXPERIMENT: an envelope wah on the front, as her attack
  or consonant, and about 30% wet flanger at maybe 178 BPM (or 178 as the flanger's pitch). `scenes/voicefx.py`, called from `sing_math.py --wah --flange rate|pitch`. The wah's band-pass opens with her loudness, mixed
  60/40 with her dry voice so consonants keep their hiss. "178" was rendered both ways: a sweep once a beat at 178 BPM, and the comb
  tuned to 178 Hz. Read from the outputs: the wah's peak moves 1.0 to 2.6 kHz on her louder frames, following her loudness at +0.75; both
  flangers swing at 2.97 Hz; the rate one's delay runs about 0.5 to 6 ms, the pitch one's centres on 183 Hz. Takes in `fx/`. ⛔ The
  tuned one is a ring at nearly one pitch that wobbles three times a second, close to what was disliked in Rei: the ear decides.
- **The whole song (11-05)**, over its instrumental. `song.syl` (26 sections, 820 sung notes) and
  `echoes.syl` (six of the seven bracketed echoes; the seventh isn't in the MIDI) are set by `midi_sing.py`, sung by
  `sing_math.py --hall`, and laid on the instrumental by `scenes/sing_mix.py`: `reva_<song>.mp3`, and `_vocal` alone.
  What the MIDI turned out to be: the sung line is the honky-tonk piano's top voice, doubled in octaves in the choruses with chord stabs
  between (so the melody is the higher note of an octave pair), and in the miracle section the grand piano carries it while the
  honky-tonk piano plays the echoes high. Its octave moves between sections; each section is put back into one register for her
  (F3 to C#5), my choice, so the choruses don't rise. The MIDI's clock is the recording's: 120 BPM, -0.035 s, the same at start, middle
  and end. Her entries land within 6 ms of that at 41.7 and 125.7 s. Pitch: 154 of 155 held notes in tune (one A#4 33 cents flat).
- ⛔ **A bug in her voice, found here and fixed in `sing_math.tracks`:** a phrase's closing fall was placed after the next note's pitch
  move whenever the rest between was shorter than the next note's opening consonants, and held that whole note 45 cents under the
  note before ("Stars" came out a semitone and a half flat). A fall now ends before the next note moves. `midi_sing.py` also joins gaps
  under 25 ms between sections, which are MIDI note-offs a hair early, not rests.
- **Version 2 (11-05)**: the original seemed to blend notes, or use chords for her voice, and in some other sections Teto only
  vocalises. The MIDI agrees: its sung line has a second voice under it in
  verse 1's and verse 2's second halves (95%, mostly a fifth below), the miracle section's second half (93%, fourths) and the choruses
  (half the notes, thirds; the rest only octave doubling). `midi_sing.py --part harmony` sings it (`harm auto|third|octave|none` per
  section), mixed 6 dB under her. Which wordless parts are Teto's: `present` tested every MIDI part against the instrumental, which
  has her voice taken out. Her lines measure +3 to +5 dB at their own pitches, the instruments +7 to +16. The four held two-note
  chords at 70, 72, 77 and 79 s measure like her (+3, +4), so REVA holds them on "ah"; the same chords in pre-chorus 2 measure like

- **Version 3 (11-05), at the WRITTEN PITCH.** v2's fault: in some spots the voice went lower where it should go higher. The big leaps

## THE TUBE: HER MOUTH BY PHYSICS (11-06, `scenes/sing_tube.py`)
On v5: the fault is her voice, not the mix. Level 3 (math) stays, rather than level 2, and there is likely better math to use
here. What the stand-in ear had pinned down (above): her vowels carry, her CONSONANTS don't, stops most of all
(3 of 36 stops that open a word), and louder or longer consonants changed nothing, so the fault was their quality. In sing_math
a consonant is a set of formant numbers sliding into the vowel with noise laid on in bands: nothing makes those numbers agree with
each other the way a real mouth's do. So her mouth is now a tube that closes, and her sound is what that tube does:
- **The shape.** 40 sections, 15 cm, a woman's neutral tract. Each vowel is the least bend of it (five cosines and a lip term,
  Levenberg-Marquardt on the tube itself) that has her formant targets, the same `VOWELS` table: all within 2% (`--shapes`), and
  the shapes came out like mouths without being told to (FLEECE narrowest at the palate with spread lips, GOOSE rounded to 0.17 cm2,
  TRAP narrowest in the pharynx). Her tongue goes straight from vowel to vowel under the consonants (Ohman 1966). A consonant is a
  constriction laid on that shape at its place and let go at a real articulator's rate (Stevens 1998: lips 100 cm2/s, tip 50,
  tongue body 25): a velar closes where her tongue body already is, with no locus table. W and Y are her tongue going to UU and IY;
  R narrows the three places that pull F3 down (lips, palate, low pharynx); L has its cavity over the tongue as a side branch.
- **The sound.** The chain-matrix solution of that tube at every harmonic, with the published losses (viscosity and heat:
  Flanagan 1972; yielding walls: Ishizaka, French & Flanagan 1975), radiation from the lips and nostrils, the nose as a branch at
  the velum. A closed mouth sounds only through its walls: a voice bar as strong as a vowel at the fundamental, 31 dB down at 1 kHz.
- **The air.** Lungs at ~7 cm H2O through the glottis and the narrowest place (the orifice law: viscous at a trickle, Bernoulli once
  it runs). Behind a closure the pressure builds as the walls give (a D: 900 -> 7000 dyn/cm2 in 45 ms) until the folds stop, and
  vents in a few ms at the release. Turbulence as Stevens measured it (source pressure ~ U^3 / A^2.5), at the constriction and at
  the glottis, a jet's spectrum, +10 dB where the jet hits the teeth; the release's own rush of air is the click.
- **Set, not measured (say so):** the turbulence gain (her S at sing_math's level, -10 dB under her vowel; then SH -8, F -18, the
  T 7 dB stronger than sing_math's weak one, all by the physics), and the glottis's damping while she voices (her neutral F1 80 Hz
  wide, as sing_math). Her close-mic presence lift is dropped: a tube has resonances all the way up, and without it her held AA
  matched sing_math's with it within 1.6 dB in every octave band.
- ⛔ Traps paid for on the way: a constriction whose middle fell between two sections never closed (a D at 0.66 cm2); a back vowel
  put the velar closure under the nose's branch (the K never closed the mouth); Bernoulli alone (U ~ sqrt) clicked at every
  phrase's first and last breath; Flanagan & Cherry's Re^2 as the strength made a T 10 dB over her vowel; a phrase's first
  consonant closing as her breath rose began "pan" with "uh-".
- Her pitch, timing, source and breathiness are sing_math's, so an A/B of the two is ONE change: her mouth.
- ⛔ More traps (11-06, after the first ear test): her voicing read the flow's kinetic pressure instead of the drop across the folds
  (every vowel at 40%, her breathiness silent); the vowel fit got KIT's formants with nearly shut lips (an S before it rang at 4 kHz,
  an SH: the fit now holds lips open for unrounded vowels, narrow for rounded); an S narrowed 2 cm in did the same (now 1.5); flat
  jet noise below its Strouhal peak made her S a whispered vowel (now it falls away on both sides); an S released at a corner, and
  a release's whole air puff, clicked ("tsk"); a slow-gliding L was heard as W (now the tip's release); her breath rising before a
  phrase's first S lengthened it 45 ms. Air flowing back as her lungs let go gave the glottis a negative resistance.
- **The stand-in ear on it (11-06, controls held: alba 15-20/26, consonant cut 0/26).** Word lists at verse speed: stops that OPEN a
  word 4-5 of 18 (v5 0 of 18), but 5/26 words overall (v5 6): K still heard as H ("can" -> "han", "cat" -> "hut": her K's frication
  is ~25 dB under her T's, its click carries it), P and D trade places with T and B. Her verses, alone, dry, three seeds: **v5 55 /
  47 / 51%, the tube 40 / 52 / 46%** (verse 1 worse on every seed, verse 2 better). Sent for listening as `ab_verses_v5_then_tube_dry.mp3`
  (v5 first) with those numbers, asking which words can't be made out in each: a listener's ears are the verdict, and on v6 they and the
  stand-in ear disagreed.
- ⛔⛔ **On that A/B (11-06): v5 is clearer, but still has a webby, flabby feel.** The tube is NOT adopted: v5
  stands, `sing_tube.py` stays in the code, unused. The next idea: compare her against a human singing voice without using that voice
  as a base, which still keeps her on the current tier. The answer, still to be confirmed: yes, on the stand-in ear's terms. **A human voice may be the RULER, never the MATERIAL:** it measures where she falls short
  and by how much; every fix still comes from published phonetics and the physics; and the ruler is several singers, never one, so
  no one person's voice can become hers (copying one singer's numbers into her would be level 2 by the back door). Candidates, licences
  to check before anything is downloaded: NUS-48E (12 singers, English songs sung AND spoken, phone-level timing; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 in
  one paper's table, so measurement only, never shipped) and VocalSet (20 professional singers, mostly vowels and techniques).
- ⭐⭐ **Both (11-06), because REVA must be able to talk as well.** Both sets are the ruler, on D: (`<data>/voice_ref/`,
  never the repo): VocalSet 1.1 (CC BY 4.0, Wilkins, Seetharaman, Wahl & Pardo, Zenodo 1442513) and NUS-48E (the Zenodo copy
  19595152, no named uploader; measurement only). And her math voice must SPEAK as well as sing: the same voice, one throat, for
  lines as well as songs. NUS-48E has every song read aloud as well as sung, so it is the ruler for her speech too.
  The plan, in order: (1) the ruler: measure the singers and readers sound by sound (consonant durations and levels, VOT, burst and
  frication spectra by place, vowel ring and breathiness, vibrato, onsets), then REVA the same way on her own songs and lines, and
  list where she falls outside the human spread; (2) fix each gap from published facts and physics, one change per A/B; (3) her
  speaking voice: text to phonemes, durations by published rules, intonation by a published model, through the same source and
  mouth.
- ⛔ **NUS-48E's own README (11-06): "This dataset is being shared with the agreement that it will be used solely for research
  purposes."** Stricter than the CC BY 4.0 on the Zenodo copy; the lab's terms govern. It is downloaded and unpacked
  (`<data>/voice_ref/nus48e/`, 12 singers, sung and read, phone-level timing) but NOT used until that is decided: ask the lab
  (Assoc. Prof. Ye Wang, NUS SMC Lab) for our use, or leave it. VocalSet (CC BY 4.0) is clear for any use with credit:
  Wilkins, Seetharaman, Wahl & Pardo, "VocalSet: A Singing Voice Dataset", ISMIR 2018.
- The ruler's first reading: all 27 of VocalSet's women's "Row, row, row your boat" (9 singers, straight, vibrato, spoken) were

- **REVA on the same ruler (v5, the women's key 329 Hz and pace, three seeds, dry; `scratchpad/ruler/`, `<data>/voice_ref/reva_row/`).**
  The ear: 44-50% (the women 100%). It gets her first half word-perfect, "Row, row, row your boat gently down the stream", then
  "merrily" x4 as "never we" (M -> N, her tapped R -> V, L -> W) and "life is" as "laugh as". The measures put numbers on webby,

  kHz against 0-2) **-20.2** / -16.1 dB: duller; loudness swing at syllable rate (4 Hz, STI's modulation depth) **0.28** / 0.50
  (0.3..0.9): under EVERY woman, her syllables run into each other; attacks 30 / 40 ms (not her fault); top (5-10 kHz) -34 / -36.
  So flabby reads as a breathy, ringless source and webby as syllables that don't separate.

  11.3 -> 7.1, ring -20.2 -> -17.3; softer sonorants (nasals .30 -> .18, liquids and glides .6-.7 -> .40): the 4 Hz swing 0.28 ->
  0.30 only; both: H1-H2 5.5, ring -16.7 (the women's median), swing 0.32. The ear unchanged (44%, the same "never we"). So the
  firmer source answers flabby by the numbers, and webby is NOT the sonorants' level: likely her notes held at one flat level

  and speed is the fault. Next: 4 = the tube with the firmer voice; then the fast passages: `layout()` shrinks every consonant by

## HER SPEAKING VOICE (11-06, `scenes/speak_math.py`)
Speech first. The method is like clean-room software: working from specs, not copying code; an open-source human voice. That is
the line exactly: the published phonetics are the SPEC, the human
recordings (VocalSet, the stand-in ear) are only the TEST SUITE, and nothing of theirs is copied in.
- Words to sounds: eSpeak NG's Scottish English (`en-gb-scotland`, the copy inside Piper: hand-written rules and a dictionary,
  no recordings), mapped onto her phonemes; her accent's own rules as `layout()` applies them (a tapped R between vowels, a sounded R
  and a dark L after one, PRICE before a voiceless consonant). Syllables by the maximal onset principle.
- Timing: Klatt 1979's duration rules (inherent and minimum lengths, clause-final lengthening, non-final shortening, polysyllabic
  and unstressed shortening, a vowel short before a voiceless consonant, clusters, the breath after a stressed P/T/K), typed from
  memory. ~5 syllables a second inside a phrase.
- Pitch: her deadpan: a baseline falling 2 semitones over the phrase, an accent on each stressed syllable each a step lower, a
  statement ending low (150 Hz from a 182 Hz baseline), a yes/no question rising 5 semitones.
- It plays through her singing voice untouched (`render(..., laid=True)`: explicit lengths per sound, no notes), either mouth; the
  physical mouth without its release clicks (the weird extra noise).
- The stand-in ear on it (10 Harvard sentences / her 3 lines): alba (control) 96 / 78%; **REVA with v5's mouth and voice 88 / 89%**;
  firmer 86 / 71%. It slips on long, fast words ("dark blue background" -> "dark blue macarons").
- ⭐ **On speech 1-3 (11-06): all sound somewhat like Miku talking; 3 is clearer in some spots, but becomes gibberish when it gets
  faster; and singing 6 is clearer in the slow parts, still rough when it gets fast.** Short
  syllables are the shared fault. Two answers, as files 4 and 5: UNHURRIED (her sheet's word): 15% under Klatt's rate (`RATE`), and
  an unstressed vowel no longer gets half its minimum (it fell to ~20 ms); SPEECH PITCH: one continuous contour (`contour()`:
  targets only at accented syllables and phrase ends, a smooth curve between) instead of a pitch held per syllable like a note,
  the likely Miku talking.
- The first speech test's last rows (controls held: alba 96 / 78, consonants cut 0 / 3): **the new mouth 59 / 71%** against v5's mouth
  88 / 89. For speech, v5's mouth is the clearer by ~30 points on the Harvard sentences.
- ⭐ **On 4 and 5 (11-06): a little better, still hard to understand; a fundamental is heard but few harmonics, and her voice
  sounds flat.** Measured on her SPEECH against VocalSet's nine women speaking
  the same words: not breathiness (her H1-H2 -0.4 dB, theirs 1.0) but her MIDDLE: 2-5 kHz 10 dB under theirs (-28 / -18.5 against
  0-2 kHz), harmonics falling -14 to -15 dB an octave (theirs ~ -10); by 1/3 octaves the gap is 0.8-4 kHz, deepest at 1.6 kHz
  (-14 dB; partly accent: her Scottish GOAT sits under the singers' American one), with extra at H1-H2 (160-400 Hz). Tenser folds
  (Fant's Rd 0.7, where her voice was 1.25) close it to -6.0 dB with the new mouth and -4.6 with v5's. ⛔ The ruler's caveat: these
  women are professional singers, likely brighter than most. Files: 6 = 5 with tenser folds, 7 = 6 through v5's mouth.
- ⭐ **File 6 sounded better (11-06; made her speaking default: `speak_math.SPEAK`, the tube without clicks, rd 0.7, breath
  .06); but the second half was very hard to understand, with no idea what she was saying, and not because of the Scottish accent,
  which a listener used to Scottish speech understands.**
  The second half is the Harvard sentences, which the listener had no text for: a fair test, and she fails it for a human. ⛔ The stand-in
  ear's Harvard scores (88% v5 mouth, 59% new mouth) are flattered: these sentences are famous and Whisper likely knows them.
  From now on the speech ruler is SEMANTICALLY UNPREDICTABLE sentences (Benoit et al. 1996: real words in a grammatical frame that
  means nothing, so no listener, human or model, can guess the words), and a listener's ear on a sentence not told beforehand.
- ⛔⛔ **THE STAND-IN EAR IS NOT A HUMAN (11-06).** On five unpredictable sentences in her clearest voice (v5's mouth, tenser folds,
  unhurried, speech pitch) a listener made out none. On twenty like them the stand-in ear (large-v3) heard 75% of her content
  words (alba 95%). It decodes her far better than a person can, so every gain it scored today was real for it and not for a person.
  A human ear is the only ruler for her speech now; the stand-in ear stays only as a smoke test.
- ⭐⭐ **Still too much like Microsoft Sam (11-06): this is being done the old way, and needs a new path found or developed.** What the pictures show (her and alba saying "Why does the kettle feed the dark
  sofa?"): every syllable a held block (her mouth jumps to a shape and stays; alba's formants never stop moving), dead silence
  between sounds where speech flows through voicing and breath, and her energy under 1 kHz where alba's lives at 1-4. Those are the
  marks of target-and-rule synthesis (Klatt's era, and Microsoft Sam's), sing_math's and the tube's control alike. The paths
  offered: a mouth that never stops moving (articulatory synthesis, VocalTractLab's published model as the spec), a listener's ear as the
  teacher (preference learning: variants, a listener picks, it learns), or level 2 after all.
- **Some field, perhaps audio synthesis or the coder scene, that no one may yet have tapped for this; the answer, ANIMATION: mouth
  physics, and it was taken up.** The reasoning:
  hearing science says people understand speech by following its MOVEMENT (three sine waves tracing a voice's formants are
  understood: sinewave speech, Remez et al. 1981; a few bands of noise following its envelope too: Shannon et al. 1995), and her
  mouth jumped and held. So her mouth is animated like her body: vowel shapes as KEYFRAMES, her tongue on animation curves through
  them, never still (`sing_tube.py` `animate`, `_hermite_keys`); glides SWELL and fade on minimum-jerk curves (Flash & Hogan 1985,
  `_bell`); stops still close and hold, as real ones do. Then two timing faults the pictures beside alba showed: fricative moves of
  50-60 ms choked the vowels around 35 ms sounds (now 25-30), and "unhurried" had slowed her consonants too: her stop closures ran
  70-130 ms to alba's 30-50 -- the dead gaps. Now only her vowels are unhurried and closures take 0.8 of Klatt's citation lengths
  (her gaps 21-59 ms). Her speaking default is the animated tube (`speak_math.SPEAK`). Cold test 2 sent.
- **A listener's ear, cold (11-06).** Test 2 (five nonsense sentences, animated mouth): only the word needle heard for sure, and
  interesting enough to keep working on (1 word of ~20). Test 3 (ten single words: map sun cake dog fish lamp rope nine ship bed)
  heard as map salt egg ball push love oooo ??? shit bed: 2 of 10, with S, SH, L, M, B heard at the start. Read as physics: the lip
  rounding for SH/R/W spread over the vowels (fish -> push, rope -> oooo); the velum port too small for a nasal to read (0.25 cm2:
  sun -> salt, nine lost); a K's jet weak (cake -> egg); an F too faint (fish -> push); an R with F2 870 Hz, a W's. Fixed together
  (each aims at different words, so test 4 shows which worked): rounding only around its consonant (25-30 ms), the port 0.45, a
  wall source for the tongue body's jet (+6 dB, Stevens), F's gap 0.07 cm2, the R's lips at 0.8. Test 4 sent (nose cat fan rain
  king top web gold shell moon). ⭐ And her FACE now comes off the same tract (`speak_math.face`: jaw, Lips_Explosive,
  Lips_Dental_Lip, Lips_Tight_O, Lips_Wide, mouthFunnel at 30 a second), animated too, since seeing her talk may help a listener
  understand her; a helper is giving scenes a per-frame named-shape track and shooting her close-up.
- ⭐⭐ **Do the animated parts make the sound, and is her face a shortcut through existing lip-sync shapes? (11-06) The aim is to
  see REVA talking and singing, with the physics visible on her as she talks.** Yes and yes: the animation IS the sound (nothing else makes it), and her face so far is a shortcut (the timing is
  the simulation's, the shapes her model's ready-made lip-sync blendshapes). What is wanted is the machine itself, visible on her.
  Step 1, `scenes/voice_view.py`: an X-ray side view of her tract drawn from the simulation every frame (each section's width, the
  velum's port, the vocal folds, the pressure behind a closure, her spectrogram under it), with her voice. Step 2 (next): the same on
  HER in the engine: a see-through cutaway of her head with that tract inside, and her jaw and lips moved by the simulation itself.
  ⭐ Step 2's data is written (not yet in the engine): `speak_math.py "<text>" OUT --face` writes the tract 30 a second beside the face
  curves; `reva_talks.py --xray --demo OUT` writes `scenes/reva_xray.scn`: her airway's 40 sections placed in her HEAD BONE's frame
  from her own mesh cut down the middle (her mouth's roof 1.645-1.656 m, its floor 1.611-1.625, her neck's front z 0.013; her model
  has no throat inside its neck, so the throat is drawn where it would be), `shp tract:NN` tracks, her phrases as captions, and a
  profile lens. The engine half (`tractsec`/`tractnose` records, tracks routed to `tractDraw`, drawn through her with the
  see-through web mode, GFX_FX_WEBX: nothing new in the renderer) is written and compiles in a copy; it waits for the hair helper's
  builds to finish before it touches the engine.
- **Cold test 4 (11-06): heard as help hell rlll kill tolp rweb fvld shell llll** for nose cat fan rain king top web gold shell moon: 1 of
  10 (shell), 2 near (top, web). ⭐ EVERY M, N and NG was heard as L. Measured: her nasal murmur and her L had the same spectrum
  (strongest ~420 Hz, as loud as the vowel, more above 1.6 kHz than her L). Her nose was one smooth 10.5 cm tube with a cheek's
  walls and no sinuses: it rang like a second mouth. THE RULER here is alba, measured, never material (`murmur_ruler.py`,
  `murmur_bands.py` in the session's scratchpad): her murmurs hump at 200-250 Hz and fall ~40 dB by 1 kHz; REVA's humped at 400.
  ⛔⛔ First rebuilt from a MAN's MRI scaled down (Pruthi, Espy-Wilson & Story 2007). **The reference material must be a woman's, not a
  man's** -- and a woman's tract is not a shrunk man's (Story, Hoffman & Titze 1997, her MRI against his: her
  pharynx ~63% of his, her mouth as long or longer). So her nose is now A WOMAN'S (`sing_tube.py` NOSE_*): her passages from women's
  acoustic rhinometry (the nostril's notch 0.55 cm2, the turbinate head's 0.47, ~1.0-1.4 behind, per side, 7.5 cm); her sinuses
  women's sizes (maxillary 14 and 15 cm3, frontal 7), their openings sized so each zero falls where a measured woman's does
  (Kitamura et al., Interspeech 2017: an 18-year-old woman's nose and sinuses from CT, printed and measured: 0.35, 0.45 and 0.7 kHz;
  hers land at 0.395, 0.51, 0.73); bone under mucosa (a quarter of a cheek's give); and the labyrinth's loss, which a straight tube
  can't make (NOSE_MAZE, growing as f squared, fitted to her measured curve). Her velum moved to a woman's: 6 cm up, not 7. Result:
  her M/N hump at 310 Hz (was 420, alba's 200-250), and against alba her murmurs now match: "moon" dull -29 dB (was -17, alba -37),
  "nose" -31 (alba -31), word-final N 12-15 dB under the vowel (alba 13-16). ⛔ The woman's measured nose peaks at 250 with the mouth
  shut; this tube at normal female anatomy gives 330 (the fit only reaches 280 with sinuses past any woman's, so it stays normal and
  says so). Her vowels were already a woman's: Peterson & Barney's women. Two more from the same test: Klatt's shortening before a voiceless consonant
  was the wrong way round in `time_phrase` (full mid-phrase, halved at a phrase's end: "top"'s vowel ran 288 ms, heard "tolp"); and
  her breath held to a phrase's last sound, so her word-final M, N and L were 4-7 dB under their vowel where alba's are 11-16: she
  now eases off over a phrase's last 0.2 s to 0.6 of her pressure as she SPEAKS (`voice["decl"]`, SPEAK's 0.4; a song holds).
  Cold test 5 went out with the man's nose and is void (renamed `..._SKIP_mans_nose.mp3`); cold test 6 sent (ten new words drawn at
  random, the woman's nose; the list in the scratchpad's `cold_6.json`, not shown to the listener).

## IT EXISTS: ADACHI REI (found 11-05)
A voice like this was suspected to exist already, though I had found no such Vocaloid. It does. Adachi Rei, by missile39, is a robot character
whose voice no person recorded. ⛔ So REVA's voice is not the first, and nothing we publish says so.

⭐ **Having listened, her voice was not much enjoyed** (11-05). So she shows it can be done and is not a sound to aim for. REVA's target stays her sheet: synthetic, sultry, sarcastic.
The reasons, which are rules for REVA: the robotic sound is overdone and hard to understand; the robot sound is an added warble at a
fixed pitch, and wobbly consonants.
- ⛔ The machine in her voice never costs a word. "Audibly a machine" is how it's built, not an effect laid on top.
- ⛔ No warble that doesn't follow the tune. As set (`VOICES["reva"]`), nothing in her sound sits at a fixed pitch. Her vibrato is 12 cents at 5 Hz, on held notes only, fading in after about a third of a second, and her pitch wander is 2 cents slow plus 0.8 fast. `reva_flat` turns all of it off, as the control.
- ⛔ Consonants hold still. Her formants wander 0.5% (`fw`) through consonants as well as vowels. That's small, but it's the dial to check first if her consonants ever sound wobbly.

What the sources say. They are mostly fan wikis. Screenshots of a wiki page settled the build, the dates and the VOCALOID status:
- **The build:** sine waves added up in Audacity, consonants from a synthesized xylophone sample, the Vocalizer plug-in, then more editing in Audacity. That page calls the result choppy and robotic. "Fully artificial and generated in Audacity" (the project's page). Moegirl's excerpt says other virtual singers were her reference. No source says how the vowels were tuned, so she's probably level 4 on our ladder, unconfirmed.
- **The dates:** production began in 2017, after missile39 built a life-sized Miku robot. Her Japanese UTAU voicebank came out on 12 October 2019. English libraries are fan-made by editing her samples by hand, one with EQ and time-stretch, without AI (project's page).
- **The AI versions:** a text-to-speech bank crowdfunded in 2021, made from her synthetic voice because there was nobody to record (VocaVerse thread); a fan-made DiffSinger bank trained on her samples, in 12 languages including English; VOCALOID 5 (stitched samples) and 6 (AI) from a campaign that began on 1 December 2025 and was fully funded. Yamaha has shown demos, with no release date yet. ⛔ No page I've read says no human-trained base model was involved. Her fan RVC banks use other voicebanks as the performance underneath, so they aren't only her.
- **The sound:** the creator wants "synthetic yet feminine" and admits parts come out screechy. Listeners called the 2019 demo rough and very hard to understand, and some liked her anyway. She has no set personality; REVA has a strong one.

Against REVA: both add up sine waves. Rei's were made into samples that UTAU stitches together; REVA's are computed fresh for each note from a glottal pulse and a tract model, with no samples and no plug-in.

What it offers us, none of it tried:
1. **Consonants from a struck sound: shelved.** Consonants are where a listener loses her words, and Rei's start from a xylophone rather than shaped noise. But that voice was not enjoyed, and nothing shows the trick makes words clearer.
2. **A level 2 with no human voice.** The fallback was AI trained on recordings. It could train on REVA's own math voice instead, as the fan DiffSinger bank did with Rei's samples, though it would inherit her flaws, and it needs a model with no human-trained base.
3. ⛔ **Her success doesn't prove ours.** She sings Japanese, which has few consonant clusters. The song this voice is for is fast English full of technical words.

Sources: https://vocaloid.fandom.com/wiki/Adachi_Rei , https://adachi-rei.carrd.co/ , https://zh.moegirl.org.cn/en/%E8%B6%B3%E7%AB%8B%E9%9B%B6 , https://vocaverse.network/threads/crowdfunding-for-a-i-voice-adachi-rei-tts-without-a-voice-provider.5986

  everything dark and L-like. Measured: her back vowels had a hole at 2-4.5 kHz. A fourth-formant aim was tried and parked (`sing_tube.F4_AIM`,
  now "none": aimed at every vowel, at the back ones, or at none, it changed nothing that matters).
- ⭐⭐ **THE RULER IS WOMEN, NOT ALBA (11-06): the aim is not to make her sound exactly like alba; better-quality voices are brought in

  Wheeler 1995, JASA 97: the h_d words, studio, 16 kHz, with their measured formants; MIT, hosted with Hillenbrand's permission at

  loud 2-4.5 kHz is against 0-1 kHz (the women's median [middle half] / REVA, dB): heed -16.7 / -24.9, hid -21.3 / -23.7, hayed -20.1 / -24.4, head

  that from her LOW F1 and F2 there (Peterson & Barney's 1952 women, AO 590/920, against these women's hawed 805/1175: lower F1 and F2 pull every
  formant above them down). ⛔ My first guess was her lips: the fit had pushed every open vowel's lips to its 9 cm2 ceiling (a woman's widest is

  of her own accent to be measured against: the VCTK corpus's Scottish women (Edinburgh, CC BY 4.0, 48 kHz studio, ~400 sentences each), which
  comes only as one ~11 GB archive: asked.

  University of Edinburgh's CSTR, CC BY 4.0): its five Scottish women, p234 (West Dumfries), p249 (Aberdeen), p262 (Edinburgh), p264 (West

  Scotland's FOOT takes its GOOSE and its PALM its TRAP. Where Peterson & Barney had her furthest off: LOT's F2 920 against their 1170, GOOSE's

  her lungs, the air's pressure and flow, turbulence; a SOFT PALATE that opens a woman's nose (rhinometry, sinuses from CT); the L's

  jaw and lips and the X-ray of her airway (`voice_view.py`, `reva_talks.py --xray`) are read off the same simulation. NOT modelled:
  a TONGUE (it exists only as the tube's shape: each vowel the smoothest bend that gives its resonances; a consonant is a squeeze
  laid on the tube at a fixed place, so her T closes at the ridge while the rest of her tongue stays where the vowel left it -- the
  women's transitions carry the consonant's place, hers barely do); TEETH (only a number: a hiss hitting them is 10 dB louder,
  Shadle 1985); a JAW; physical VOCAL FOLDS (her buzz is the LF pulse, a shape of mathematics, the same every cycle). How far it can
  go, each a published method: (1) an articulatory model -- a tongue (tip, body, root), jaw, lips, velum and teeth placed from a
  WOMAN's MRI, the airway computed from where they are, so a consonant is a whole tongue moving and the teeth shape her S and T, and the
  same articulators drive her face and X-ray; (2) physical vocal folds (two-mass, Ishizaka & Flanagan 1972; body-cover, Story & Titze
  1995): her buzz from air pushing tissue, voice that starts as a real voice starts (the 14-25 ms after B, D, G she lacks), folds and
  airway acting on each other; (3) the airway's sound in 3D on the GPU: past ~4 kHz a one-dimensional tube is wrong (cross-modes,
  more loss), which is her too-bright top end; (4) a tongue moved by muscles (finite elements): research-grade, the far end.

## HER BODY: AN ANDROID'S VOICE, BUILT LIKE A WOMAN'S (11-06)
⭐⭐ **REVA is an android, not a robot, and there is a difference**; **a little robotic is okay, but not the goal: a fully
synthesized voice is the goal**; and on how far the physics can go: **all of the steps, and lungs too**. An android is made to pass as
human: the machine is in how she is built (a body like a woman's, all of it math and physics, no recording at any step), not in how
she sounds. Every part from measurements of WOMEN. The order, each step built, tried once, and handed to the ear as its own file:
1. **LUNGS AND WINDPIPE.** (a) ✅ her windpipe under her glottis (below). (b) her lungs as a volume she speaks out of: breaths taken
   between phrases (heard), the pressure from their recoil and her breathing muscles, phrases as long as her air (women's speech
   breathing: Hoit, Hixon, Altman & Morgan 1989, 30 women; Winkworth et al. 1994). Needs air that can flow IN (`aero` assumes out).
2. **HER AIRWAY SAMPLE BY SAMPLE.** The tube solved in time (a transmission line with the same losses, nose and side branches), not
   harmonic by harmonic, so the air can push back on her folds. A compiled core if numpy is too slow.
3. **PHYSICAL VOCAL FOLDS.** A body-cover model (Story & Titze 1995) driven by her laryngeal muscles (Titze & Story 2002's rules; the
   triangular body-cover model, Alzamendi et al. 2021, open on arXiv 2108.01115) at a woman's fold length and mass, between her
   windpipe and her airway. Her voice starts and stops as a voice does (the 14-25 ms after a B, D, G she lacks) and varies a little.
4. **TONGUE, JAW, LIPS, TEETH, VELUM.** An articulatory model of a woman's mouth: Story, Titze & Hoffman 1998 (JASA 104: a 27-year-old
   woman's MRI, ten vowels, L and R, as area functions) and the USC 75-Speaker Speech MRI Database (Lim et al. 2021, Scientific Data;
   CC BY 4.0, figshare 13725546: its WOMEN's static anatomy and real-time MRI of them speaking). Her airway from where they are; a
   consonant a whole tongue moving; teeth for S, T, TH; her face and X-ray driven by the same articulators.
5. **HER AIRWAY'S SOUND IN 3D,** on the GPU (finite differences on her articulators' 3D shape): above ~4 kHz.
6. **MUSCLES:** her tongue and jaw moved by muscles (finite elements). Research-grade: the far end.

every speaker's static upper-airway MRI), `dataset_2drt_video_only.zip` (2.55 GB: their real-time MRI videos with audio); peak ~10 GB

by range later).

- **VocalTractLab (Peter Birkholz, TU Dresden)**: an articulatory synthesizer, open source under the GNU
  GPL since 2.3 (2.4, 5 Dec 2025, on vocaltractlab.de): its code can't come into reva or the kit (MIT), its published methods can,
  clean room. Birkholz 2013 (PLoS ONE 8(4): e60603), "Modeling consonant-vowel coarticulation": every consonant's tract shape is
  made in three contexts, /a/ /i/ /u/, and a consonant before any vowel is their mix, weighted by where that vowel sits among the
  three (an SVD pseudo-inverse, clamped to the triangle; the lips weighted on their own so rounding moves apart from the tongue).
  "gee, gaa, goo" IS the model's own grid. His /g/ scored best of the stops (VOT 38 ms against /b/ 18, /d/ 22); consonants 82.4%
  heard right in syllables against ~98% natural; fitted to one German speaker's MRI (one speaker: the 11-07 objection to one person's
  tract applies to the data, not the method).
- ⛔ **If it already does it, it does it poorly.** Looked at (the scratchpad's `velar_sheet.py`: her babble's first
  syllables beside Scottish women's "give, gods, go, kids, call, could", spectrograms 0-6 kHz): four faults in her G and K. (1) her G
  HUMMED through its closure ~50 ms (the voice bar), "mm-ga"; theirs are silent until the crack; (2) her release had almost no
  BURST, where every woman's opens with a crack across the whole picture; (3) her vowel SNAPPED on, flat from the release, where
  theirs bend into it over 30-50 ms; (4) her K's BREATH was a ~15 ms blob, theirs 40-80 ms of loud breath already shaped like the
  vowel. **Fixed, each a voice key, off = v5 bit-exact:** `quiet_closures` (s: a syllable-opening B/D/G
  closes silent, her voice ramps in that long after the crack), `crack` (dB: 3 ms, 0.4-9 kHz at the release; -40 off) and
  `burst_gain` (dB on every burst), `bend` (s: the move out of a stop or nasal into the vowel, was 16 ms), `asp_gain` (x the breath
  after an opening P/T/K; its length is `floors`'). On the desk as CONSONANT FIXES; the built-in voice **"babble fixes"** = file 6 +
  quiet 15 ms, crack -8, burst +6, bend 45 ms, breath x1.8 -- MY values, a start for the ear. Drawn again: the hum gone, the crack
  there on G and K; her K's breath still ~40 ms and the bend hard to see: the two to dial by ear.

- ⭐ **CHIMERA, by Jameson Hodge (11-10).** An open-source voice synthesizer
  made the way hers is: air through a simulated airway (lungs, folds, a branched tract, lips, nose), its README's "No samples, no
  neural audio"; speech, singing, beatboxing and a few animals. github.com/jamesondh/chimera-vocal-synth, MIT (so its code CAN come
  into reva and the kit with credit, where VocalTractLab's GPL can't); the app runs in a browser at chimera-vocal-synth.vercel.app.
  Read through a fetch agent: the repo page, `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/rust-engine.md` (dated 2026-11-05); NOT the code, not
  the app's own text, and nobody here has heard it. What its docs say, against hers:
  THE SAME: a time-domain airway with yielding walls and a nose, hiss from the air's own Reynolds number with a source at the lower
  teeth, bursts from pressure let go, CMUdict and Klatt's durations, real speech used only to compare against (TSP, 23 speakers).
  WHAT IT HAS AND SHE DOESN'T: (1) a TONGUE AND JAW -- named articulators (jaw, tongue body x/y, tip, groove, lips, velum, larynx)
  on a 2D mid-sagittal outline turned to areas, driven by GESTURES (Articulatory Phonology): the tongue body moves vowel to vowel
  THROUGH the consonants (Ohman), a consonant laid over it, each articulator a critically damped spring at its own speed; hers is a
  fitted tube squeezed at fixed places (step 6 of her build, re-scoped). (2) REAL TIME: its Rust engine at 96 kHz inside takes
  about a fifth of one core; hers takes 3.5 times as long to make as it lasts. (3) Its glottis is an AREA pulse (open and closing
  phases, a chink, jitter, shimmer, fry) and the flow comes out of the airway: between her LF "speaker" and the folds turned
  down by ear.
  ⛔ WHAT ISN'T HERS TO TAKE: its woman's BODY is the man's template scaled by four hand-set numbers -- never a man scaled down
  (11-06). (Corrected after reading the code: its design doc says its vowels are fitted to Hillenbrand's MALE means, and I
  said so; `vowel_data.rs` fits the female body's twelve English vowels to Hillenbrand's WOMEN.) Its methods and code are usable; a
  woman's numbers stay the women's (her 22, the scans' middle).
  ⭐ **STUDIED** (a study kept with her, not in this repository) -- its code read part by part against hers, where each stands by
  its own ruler (her hisses are nearer women's than its female voice's; it is ahead in everything a tongue gives and in speed), and
  what to take, in order: its closing rule (for her pops), its fast-passage rule (for her fast verses), one airway run not two
  (REVA CHAT's wait), its measuring loop (whole sentences, an aligner, costs in the women's own spread), then a tongue and jaw on
  women's numbers. Nothing of it built or run; nobody here has heard it.
  ⛔ A crypto token calling itself CHIMERA rides its name: nothing to do with the software.
